Is AMD Stock a Buy as AI Revenue Soars?

Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ: AMD) turned in strong third-quarter results, as its data center revenue nearly doubled. The semiconductor stock has had a strong year, up over 125% going into the report, but has more recently been caught in the AI infrastructure sell-off, and it also took a hit because of rival Intel's (NASDAQ: INTC) weak guidance.

Let's take a closer look at the company's earnings results and prospects to see why I think the stock is a buy.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Strong AI growth ahead

While AMD and Intel are both competitors in the central processing unit (CPU) space, the two companies are quite different. AMD has been taking share from Intel in the server CPU market for years, and has also begun making inroads with its graphics processing units (GPUs). As such, AMD is much more about serving data center clients, while Intel is much more heavily exposed to the weakening PC market, which has come under pressure from rising memory costs.

AMD is seeing pressure in this area as well, projecting a double-digit percentage decline in unit shipments in the PC market next year. Overall, its client and gaming segment revenue fell 8% to $3.7 billion. Client revenue, where its PC business sits, rose 7% to $2.9 billion, while gaming revenue fell 40% to $773 million.

AMD's biggest unit and growth driver, however, is its data center segment. This accounted for 64% of its Q3 revenue, and the company projected it will represent more than 80% of its revenue in 2027.

AMD's data center revenue surged 97% in Q3 to $8.5 billion, powered by strong demand for its Epyc CPUs and MI450 GPUs. The company began shipping its new Venice CPUs in the quarter, which it expects will help it gain even more market share. It continues to see the server CPU market growing to a $220 billion total addressable market by 2030, as demand surges due to the rise of AI agents.

At the same time, the company said AI labs, hyperscalers, and cloud computing providers all increased GPU deployments, helping drive record revenue. It said it delivered its Helios full-rack AI system, which combines its GPUs, CPUs, and networking components, this quarter to lead customers, including Anthropic, Meta Platforms, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Oracle. It said it expects Helios revenue to ramp up in Q4 as OEM (original equipment manufacturer) and ODM (original design manufacturer) partners begin to ship the systems.

title: Advanced Micro Devices vs. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing: The AI Sell-Off Is Exposing a Critical Difference Investors Shouldn't Ignore for 2027

Advanced Micro Devices vs. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing: The AI Sell-Off Is Exposing a Critical Difference Investors Shouldn't Ignore for 2027
RJ Fulton, The Motley Fool
Thu, November 5, 2026 at 12:20 PM PST 6 min read
AMD
TSM
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

The artificial intelligence (AI) boom has propelled semiconductor stocks to new heights, but recent selling pressure has raised questions about elevated valuations and the sustainability of massive AI infrastructure spending. For investors looking toward 2027, the pullback presents an opportunity to reassess two of the industry's leading players: Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (NYSE:TSM).

While AMD competes to capture a larger share of the AI chip market with its advanced processors and GPUs, TSMC manufactures the cutting-edge chips that power much of the industry. Both stand to benefit from continued AI investment, but their distinct business models, financial strength, and valuations could lead to very different outcomes as the market becomes increasingly selective.

The case for Advanced Micro Devices

AMD designs high-performance processors and graphics chips used in data centers, personal computers, gaming systems, and embedded applications. The company has emerged as a leading challenger to Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) in the AI accelerator market, supported by growing demand for its EPYC server processors and Instinct GPUs. Its multiyear partnership with OpenAI represents a significant opportunity to expand its presence in AI infrastructure, although competition remains intense.

AMD's financial performance reflects this momentum. In fiscal 2025, revenue climbed 34% to $34.6 billion, while net income reached $4.3 billion, representing a profit margin of approximately 12.5%. Data center revenue grew 32% to $16.6 billion, driven by strong demand for server processors and AI accelerators.

At the end of 2025, its debt-to-equity ratio stood at approximately 0.1x, with a current ratio of 2.9x, providing considerable financial flexibility. AMD generated $5.5 billion in free cash flow during the year, more than doubling its 2024 total. However, stock-based compensation of approximately $1.6 billion represented a meaningful portion of operating cash flow, introducing potential shareholder dilution.

The case for Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing

TSMC is the world's leading contract chip manufacturer. Unlike chip designers who compete for market share, TSMC benefits from manufacturing the processors that power much of the AI industry. In 2025, the company produced more than 12,600 products for 534 customers, providing broad exposure to demand across AI infrastructure, smartphones, and automotive markets.

TSMC's financial performance reflects its dominant position. In fiscal 2025, revenue climbed 35.9% to $122.4 billion, while net income reached $55.2 billion, representing an impressive profit margin of 45.1%. High-performance computing accounted for approximately 58% of revenue, supported by strong demand for advanced processors and AI infrastructure.

Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) stock is down 15.1% as of 2:38 a.m. ET on Thursday, Nov. 5, after a midterm victory for Democrats set off a sell-off in chip stocks.

The S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) and the Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC) are down 3.9% and 5.0%, respectively.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Why AMD stock is falling in the chip stock sell-off

Two days after the momentous election, investors are dumping chipmakers, worried that a Democratic Congress will clamp down on the AI industry. The risk to the data center build-out is actually greater at the state level: new governors in Texas, Ohio, and Georgia campaigned partly on data center moratoriums. These are key states for AI construction.

Image source: AMD.

If these moratoriums are put in place, the AI capex flows that have fueled the extreme growth of AMD and other chipmakers could slow.

The iShares Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SOXX) is down 7.5% so far today.

AMD earnings were strong, but data center timing is the question

AMD reported its Q3 results on Tuesday afternoon, with sales up 45%, hitting $13.4 billion. Data Center revenue nearly doubled. The question investors are asking is whether the data centers that buy AMD's chips get built as fast as everyone planned. And if that happens, how does AMD keep growing at the pace investors have come to expect?

title: US stocks nosedive as Democrat victory sparks investor panic

US stocks nosedive as Democrat victory sparks investor panic

^NDX

Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Tech stocks sank at the open on Wall Street - REUTERS/Jeenah Moon

Wall Street suffered its worst sell-off since Donald Trump's tariff rollout amid fears the Democrats will derail the AI boom.

The Nasdaq 100 plunged more than 6pc on Thursday - the biggest fall since April 2025 - with shares in semiconductor makers the hardest hit.

The downturn was the worst since Mr Trump's so-called "liberation day", when he rolled out tariffs to countries around the world.

Investors fear the Democrats' midterm election victory will usher in tighter restrictions on AI companies, whose valuations have grown rapidly under Mr Trump.

Nvidia, which is the world's most valuable listed company, fell by more than 6pc while rivals including AMD and Micron plummeted 13pc and 11pc, respectively.

The companies make semiconductors that are used in data centres – huge buildings that power the models of AI companies.

Several Democrats which have won control of former Republican states have backed moratoriums on data centres in their local areas, potentially signalling a slowdown in demand for chips.

Elon Musk's empire also took a beating for a second day, with Tesla plunging 10pc and SpaceX falling 9pc.

The decline on Wall Street was in stark contrast to European markets. The FTSE 100 was 0.5pc higher, while the Cac 40 in Paris gained 0.7pc as investors switched out from AI stocks into more traditional industries.

Susannah Streeter, an analyst at Wealth Club, said: "A release valve has been unscrewed following the Democratic success of the midterms, with pent-up concerns about an escalation of the war in the Middle East evaporating.

"But sentiment around the AI trade remains fragile, with an expected slowdown in the data centre build-out still acting like a drag on the big tech sector players."

This article first appeared on GuruFocus.

Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) sank 12.68% to $426.79 at 10:10 a.m. ET in November 5 regular trading. The chip designer's November 3 earnings report pointed to another sharp revenue acceleration, but investors were selling hard. The retreat, also reflected in session data, puts the spotlight on a tougher question: how much profit can AMD squeeze from its AI expansion?

Warning! GuruFocus has detected 5 Warning Signs with AMD.

AMD GF Value chart

Quarterly revenue reached $13.377 billion, with data-center revenue of approximately $8.5 billion, up 97% from a year earlier. AMD forecast December-quarter revenue of $17 billion, plus or minus 3%, implying roughly 27% sequential growth at the midpoint. The catch is margins. Its non-GAAP gross margin forecast of approximately 55% sits below the reported quarter's 56%, suggesting the next wave of sales could arrive with less profit per revenue dollar.

The GuruFocus snapshot adds a valuation warning to that growth story. AMD's GF Score of 81/100 comes with strong growth and momentum readings, but a weak GF Value reading and a price-to-earnings ratio of 92.8 suggest expectations remain demanding despite the selloff. Rapid expansion alone may not be enough to steady sentiment. AMD needs to turn its growing systems business into stronger earnings and cash generation while keeping costs under control.
